title: Writing an LLM from scratch, part 3
summary: Wrangling data so that it can be handled by an LLM, plus token and position embeddings.
markdown:
I'm reading [Sebastian Raschka](https://sebastianraschka.com/)'s book "[Build a Large Language Model (from Scratch)](https://www.manning.com/books/build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch)", and posting about what I found interesting every day that I read some of it.

[Here's a link to the previous post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2).

Today I was working through the second half of Chapter 2, "Working with text data", which I'd started just before Christmas. Only two days off, so it was reasonably fresh in my mind :-)

### Data sampling with a sliding window

The first section is about how we take a relatively unstructured document -- the book uses "The Verdict" by Edith Wharton -- and turn it into structured data that we can feed into an LLM so that it can predict the next word and be trained to do so with reasonable accuracy.

There's nothing conceptually difficult in this section, but I did find myself with some unanswered questions and a little bit of confusion. Let's work through it.

The goal of our LLM is to take some context and predict the next word (strictly, token). Let's say that the text that we're training it on is just

```
Once more unto the breach
```

We might want to train it on examples like this (written `input_token_list -> target_output_token`)

```
["Once"] -> "more"
["Once", "more"] -> "unto"
["Once", "more", "unto"] -> "the"
["Once", "more", "unto", "the"] -> "breach"
```

The book goes through some simple code to do exactly that kind of thing, and that's all pretty clear.

It's left implicit, but I also get the impression that we'd normally be using fixed input sizes. Let's say that this was three, then that sample input sentence would give us just two training samples:

```
["Once", "more", "unto"] -> "the"
["more", "unto", "the"] -> "breach"
```

(Later it's mentioned that we try to avoid overlaps between training samples, so that might not be strictly accurate -- but you can imagine how it would work if the training text was longer.)

Up to this point, everything was crystal-clear to me :-)

But then things changed, and it wasn't clear to me why this was. It has the feel of something that will become clear later, but at this point I am a bit confused.

The sentence that introduces the change is "we are interested in returning two tensors: an input tensor containing the text the LLM sees, and a target tensor that *includes the targets* for the LLM to predict" (italics mine). The target has become pluralised and is only *included* in the target tensor rather than being its sole element.

What this means is that we switch so that the target is a list of the same length as the input, but starting with the second element from the input and including the word that comes next -- the one we're trying to predict. To make that more concrete, let's say we were targetting an input size of three tokens like we were above -- we change to having training data that looks like this:

```
["Once", "more", "unto"] -> ["more", "unto", "the"]
["more", "unto", "the"] -> ["unto", "the", "breach"]
```

It's pretty clearly the same data as before with some extra stuff in the target, and the code to generate it is simple and easy to understand. I just don't understand *why* we're adding on the extra leading elements at this stage. It will doubtless become clearer later! I'm just confused right now. However, I've decided I'm going to follow a strict "no side quests" rule while reading this book, so it will have to remain a mystery for now. [1](#fn-1)

Anyway, having established this data format, Raschka introduces some code to create a PyTorch `Dataset` subclass that can generate it for us. It's called `GPTDatasetV1`, so presumably will be enhanced later on -- in particular, I noted that it loads all of the text into memory, which would have to change with larger amounts of data. Anyway, the `GPTDatasetV1` has as its parameters that text, a tokenizer, and two more interesting params:

-   `max_length`; the length of our input sequences (and thus of the target sequences)
-   `stride`, which is the gaps between the starts of those lists in the original text.

I was finding it a bit hard to understand how these interacted at the edge cases. For example, considering

```
1 2 3 4 5 6
```

..with a max length of 3 and a stride also of 3, it clearly splits into two potential input lists, `1 2 3` and `4 5 6`. But given that we need, for each of these input lists, a target list which is the second and third elements from the original input list and then the next one from the original sequence, what do we do at the end? There's no element after `6` to put into a target sequence.

Playing with things in IPython made it clear what happens (at least, with a bit of fiddling with PyTorch docs in order to find out how to convert `tensor([[ 16, 362, 513]])` into a list I could pass to the tokenenizer to decode):

`In [135]: for stride in range(1, 4):      ...:     print(f"\nWith stride={stride}:")      ...:     dataloader = create_dataloader_v1("1 2 3 4 5 6", batch_size=1, max_length=3, stride=stride, shuffle=False)      ...:     for inputs, target in iter(dataloader):      ...:         print(tokenizer.decode(inputs[0].tolist()), " --> ", tokenizer.decode(target[0].tolist()))      ...:  With stride=1: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4  2 3 4  -->   3 4 5  3 4 5  -->   4 5 6  With stride=2: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4  3 4 5  -->   4 5 6  With stride=3: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4`

So, if it can't generate a target list of the given size, it won't output a input/target pair at all. To double-check what happens with one extra element in the input list:

`In [137]: for stride in range(1, 4):      ...:     print(f"\nWith stride={stride}:")      ...:     dataloader = create_dataloader_v1("1 2 3 4 5 6 7", batch_size=1, max_length=3, stride=stride, shuffle=False)      ...:     for inputs, target in iter(dataloader):      ...:         print(tokenizer.decode(inputs[0].tolist()), " --> ", tokenizer.decode(target[0].tolist()))      ...:  With stride=1: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4  2 3 4  -->   3 4 5  3 4 5  -->   4 5 6  4 5 6  -->   5 6 7  With stride=2: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4  3 4 5  -->   4 5 6  With stride=3: 1 2 3  -->   2 3 4  4 5 6  -->   5 6 7`

So that's pretty clear.

(One interesting thing to note is the extra spaces before the numbers after `1` -- as I noted [last time](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2), tokenizers tend to have separate tokens for, say, `"2"`, and `" 2"`. Due to the structure of my input string, it chose the without-space one for 1, and the with-space ones for the other numbers.)

Anyway -- apart from my ongoing confusion about why the target isn't just the next word that we want the LLM to predict, but instead all of the words in the input apart from the first one, plus the next word at the end, all of this seemed pretty logical and clear.

The next steps were just explaining how you could get the dataloader to provide batches (something I was familiar with from [my fine-tuning experiments](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)).

For anyone that's reading this that doesn't already know, when you feed an input into a neural network, it's a vector, but you can also feed in a matrix -- that is, a bunch of inputs simultaneously. So, for a single input you're essentially feeding in a 1 x *n* matrix -- one row, *n* columns, where *n* is the number of inputs to the neural network. But if you feed in a *b* x *n* matrix, with *b* separate inputs, one on each row, the maths is exactly the same and the code doesn't need changing.

This takes up more memory and processor power to do the calculations and get an output, but running (say) a batch of 8 inputs and getting 8 outputs in one go is less expensive in processing time than going through the full calculations 8 times, once for each input. In particular, when you're training, you can save quite a lot of time doing batches -- so long as you have enough RAM (or more likely, VRAM) to hold them.

There was an interesting side note about this, though -- Raschka mentions that "small batch sizes require less memory during training but lead to more noisy model updates" -- I'd certainly seen the memory effects of batch sizes during my fine tuning experiments, and (during a conversation with Claude when looking into [gradient checkpointing](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)) got the impression that larger batches might lead to better-generalised models:

> \[A\]pparently, larger batch sizes can lead to better, more generalised training. Intuitively this makes sense. For an LLM, you can imagine that training it on the sentence "I like bacon", and then "I like cheese", and then "I like eggs", adjusting the weights after each one, might lead it to "learn" more from the first example than from the second, and more from the second than the third. Training on a batch of all three of them in one go and then doing a single adjustment of the weights afterwards seems like it might consider them all more equally.

It was good to read some confirmation of this underlying process (though I'm sure my analogy is absurdly simplified).

The other thing that I found interesting was a mention that we would normally try to avoid overlap between batches to avoid overfitting. That sounds to me (and perhaps I'm misunderstanding) like in practice the `max_length` and the `stride` would be set to the same number.

Anyway, that ended the section on setting up the dataset for training. Now it was on to the section on token embeddings.

### Token embeddings

This one I was expecting to be really tricky -- how do you work out embeddings for each of the tokens in your vocabulary, or at least, how do you put things in place so that you can train them? But I was forgetting that because the embeddings are trained as part of the general LLM training, all we really needed to put in place was the infrastructure for that.

One interesting thing that came out of this and the various notes was why we use embeddings at all. It's relatively easy to see why you can't just feed in token IDs directly -- they're discrete numbers that don't really mean anything in and of themselves. Neural nets work best when they're dealing with some kind of continuous data, where (say) 1.5 really does mean something halfway between 1 and 2. But if "once" is token 123, and "more" is token 124, what does 123.5 mean? Nothing meaningful.

I'd read in the past about "one-hot" encodings to work around issues like this, where you have discrete inputs. That's where you have a vector of length *n*, where *n* is the number of options for a choice -- you fill it with zeros, apart from one specific element that is 1, representing the particular choice in this case. It crops up in Jeremy Howard's Fast.AI course, for example -- IIRC it's specifically the case where he's working through building a system to predict who survived the Titanic, and one of the features he's looking at is the class of the passenger: first, second or third. He explains that this is a bad feature, because there's no (for example) 2.5th class, so he creates new `is_first_class`, `is_second_class`, and `is_third_class` synthetic features. You can think of that as being adding on a new feature `class` which is a vector with three elements, which is set to `[1, 0, 0]` for first class, `[0, 1, 0]` for second, and `[0, 0, 1]` for third. That is more meaningful because fractions start meaning something. Let's say that your model wanted to express "second class passengers were more likely to survive, then first, then third", it could multiply the passenger's one-hot encoded `class` vector by `[0.3, 0.5, 0.1]`.

So, I'd had a vague thought in the past that perhaps LLMs received each token as a one-hot vector -- that is, each token was a vector as long as the vocab size, with a single `1` in the position related to its token ID, and `0`s everywhere else. This would then be fed into the LLM, which could make better sense of them. Let's say that token 1001 was "also" and 3109 was "additionally" -- they have very similar meanings, and some part of the network that was trying to deal with that kind of concept could have weights that were high for the 1001st and 3109th positions in these one-hot vectors and low everywhere else.

However, in a side note, Raschka points out that this is essentially the same as the embedding system. If you take those one-hot vectors and pass them through a single fully-connected layer of neurons, you are performing the same calculations as you would to generate the embeddings. So -- embeddings here are just a neat way of creating an easily-trainable input layer. This makes a lot of intuitive sense to me, but I need to think it through to make sure I really do understand it -- something about it feels like there's an extra order involved -- order in the sense that vectors are order 1, matrices order 2, and so on -- that doesn't exactly match my mental model of how data flows through a neural network. But still, an intuitive "OK, that sort of kind of makes sense" is what I need right now.

All that aside: the goal with embeddings was to have a set of vectors of some particular dimensionality (you might remember from the [last post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2) that the 124M parameter GPT-2's had 768 dimensions and GPT-3 had 12,288). Each token would have one specific vector associated with it, so the process for getting the text into the LLM would look something like this pseudocode:

`tokens = tokenizer.encode(input_text) embeddings = [embeddings_dict[token] for token in tokens] result = do_LLM(embeddings)`

...where `embeddings_dict` would just have a map from each token ID to its associated embedding vector. Indeed, when I started reading the explanatory text I was expecting to see exactly that code -- a bunch of PyTorch vectors, each with the `requires_grad` property set to make them trainable.

As it turns out, though, PyTorch has a `torch.nn.Embedding` class that handles that for you. From [the docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Embedding.html) it looks like it's not much more than a wrapper around the kind of dictionary I was thinking about -- though I can easily imagine that having it exist as a more abstract entity allows optimisations that make it faster than a lower-level implementation would.

So, the code that Rashka goes through gives a few simple examples with low numbers of dimensions just to make the concepts clear.

And next, it was on to encoding token positions.

### Encoding word positions

The core here is that the self-attention mechanism (that magical thing I'm so looking forward to learning about!) does not apparently "understand" the concept of ordering -- if it gets the same token twice in a stream it will treat it the same way each time. So in:

```
The cat ate the Christmas turkey
```

...the two "the"s would be treated the same, which is obviously not what we want, as they relate to "cat" and "Christmas turkey" respectively.

So once we've worked out encodings for each token, we also need to add on information about where they are in the input. These are called position embeddings, there are two flavours -- relative and absolute -- and we simply add them element-wise to the token embeddings. It's not explained how relative position embeddings work in practice (another interesting side quest I'm very carefully avoiding), but for absolute ones, we just need another dict (or it might as well be a list) mapping from the index of a token in the input stream to a vector -- that is, position 1 in the input will always have the same position embedding, position 2 its own different one, and so on. This, of course, gives us a hard cap on the number of tokens we can accept (one of the reasons LLMs tend to have a fixed context window, I imagine). But it's simple, and apparently OpenAI's GPT models use it, so it's presumably a good way to do things :-)

Here's some sample pseudocode:

`tokens = tokenizer.encode(input_text) token_embeddings = [token_embeddings_dict[token] for token in tokens] position_embeddings = [position_embeddings_list[ii] for ii in range(len(tokens))] input_embeddings = [(te + pe) for (te, pe) in zip(token_embeddings, position_embeddings)] result = do_LLM(input_embeddings)`

That means that the position embeddings need to be the same dimensionality as the token embeddings, of course (because otherwise we can't do the element-wise additions in the calculations of `input_embeddings`).

But again, these are things that are trained as part of the LLM training, so we just start off with arbitrary numbers in the embedding vectors for each position -- ~say all-ones for the one for position 1, all 2s for position 2, and so on~ \[NOTE: they really are arbitrary, of the same scale as the token embeddings -- see comments below for why my original example was confusing\]. Training will adjust them appropriately.

### Summary

Apart from my ongoing confusion about the targets in our dataset being lists with the next token to predict at the end rather than just the next token, I think that was all pretty clear to me, and hopefully my notes are reasonably clear too :-)

I'm fighting hard to resist the temptation to read up on that, anyway, as I've given myself strict "no side quests" instructions for this run through the book. If I still don't understand it at the end, then I'll definitely be reading up on it.

Next time around, it's chapter 3 -- attention mechanisms. Definitely looking forward to that one!

[Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-4).

* * *

To double-check what happens with one extra element in the input list: 所以，如果无法生成指定大小的目标列表，它就完全不会输出这一对输入/目标。为了再次确认输入列表多一个元素时的情况： `In [137]: for stride in range(1, 4): ...: print(f"\nWith stride={stride}:") ...: dataloader = create_dataloader_v1("1 2 3 4 5 6 7", batch_size=1, max_length=3, stride=stride, shuffle=False) ...: for inputs, target in iter(dataloader): ...: print(tokenizer.decode(inputs[0].tolist()), " --> ", tokenizer.decode(target[0].tolist())) ...: With stride=1: 1 2 3 --> 2 3 4 2 3 4 --> 3 4 5 3 4 5 --> 4 5 6 4 5 6 --> 5 6 7 With stride=2: 1 2 3 --> 2 3 4 3 4 5 --> 4 5 6 With stride=3: 1 2 3 --> 2 3 4 4 5 6 --> 5 6 7` So that's pretty clear. 这样就很清楚了。 (One interesting thing to note is the extra spaces before the numbers after `1` -- as I noted [last time](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2), tokenizers tend to have separate tokens for, say, `"2"`, and `" 2"`. Due to the structure of my input string, it chose the without-space one for 1, and the with-space ones for the other numbers.) （值得注意的一点是，数字 `1` 后面出现了额外空格——正如我在[上一篇](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2)中提到的，分词器往往会分别为 `"2"` 和 `" 2"` 设置词元。由于输入字符串的结构，它给 `1` 选择了不带空格的词元，而其他数字选择了带空格的词元。） Anyway -- apart from my ongoing confusion about why the target isn't just the next word that we want the LLM to predict, but instead all of the words in the input apart from the first one, plus the next word at the end, all of this seemed pretty logical and clear. 总之，除了我一直困惑为什么目标不是 LLM 要预测的下一个词，而是输入中除第一个词之外的所有词，再加上末尾的下一个词以外，其余内容都很有逻辑，也很清楚。 The next steps were just explaining how you could get the dataloader to provide batches (something I was familiar with from [my fine-tuning experiments](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)). 接下来只是解释如何让数据加载器提供批次（这部分我在[微调实验](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)中已经熟悉了）。 For anyone that's reading this that doesn't already know, when you feed an input into a neural network, it's a vector, but you can also feed in a matrix -- that is, a bunch of inputs simultaneously. So, for a single input you're essentially feeding in a 1 x *n* matrix -- one row, *n* columns, where *n* is the number of inputs to the neural network. But if you feed in a *b* x *n* matrix, with *b* separate inputs, one on each row, the maths is exactly the same and the code doesn't need changing. 如果你还不了解：向神经网络输入数据时，输入是一个向量，但也可以输入一个矩阵——也就是同时输入一批数据。因此单个输入本质上是一个 1×*n* 矩阵——一行、*n* 列，其中 *n* 是输入神经网络的数量。如果输入一个 *b*×*n* 矩阵，每行放一个独立输入，数学运算完全相同，代码也不需要改变。 This takes up more memory and processor power to do the calculations and get an output, but running (say) a batch of 8 inputs and getting 8 outputs in one go is less expensive in processing time than going through the full calculations 8 times, once for each input. In particular, when you're training, you can save quite a lot of time doing batches -- so long as you have enough RAM (or more likely, VRAM) to hold them. 这样做会占用更多内存和处理能力来完成计算并得到输出，但一次运行（比如）包含 8 个输入的批次并得到 8 个输出，在处理时间上比把完整计算做 8 次、每个输入做一次更省。尤其在训练时，只要 RAM（更可能是 VRAM）足够容纳它们，使用批次可以节省很多时间。 There was an interesting side note about this, though -- Raschka mentions that "small batch sizes require less memory during training but lead to more noisy model updates" -- I'd certainly seen the memory effects of batch sizes during my fine tuning experiments, and (during a conversation with Claude when looking into [gradient checkpointing](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)) got the impression that larger batches might lead to better-generalised models: 不过这里有个有趣的旁注——Raschka 提到“较小的批次大小在训练时需要更少内存，但会导致模型更新更加嘈杂”。我在微调实验中当然见过批次大小对内存的影响；在和 Claude 讨论[梯度检查点](https://www.gilesthomas.com/fine-tuning)时，我还得到这样的印象：更大的批次可能产生泛化更好的模型： > \[A\]pparently, larger batch sizes can lead to better, more generalised training. Intuitively this makes sense. For an LLM, you can imagine that training it on the sentence "I like bacon", and then "I like cheese", and then "I like eggs", adjusting the weights after each one, might lead it to "learn" more from the first example than from the second, and more from the second than the third. Training on a batch of all three of them in one go and then doing a single adjustment of the weights afterwards seems like it might consider them all more equally. 显然，更大的批次大小可能带来更好、泛化性更强的训练。直觉上这很合理。对于 LLM，你可以想象先用“I like bacon”训练，再用“I like cheese”，再用“I like eggs”，每次都调整权重；这样它从第一个例子中“学到”的可能比第二个多，从第二个学到的又比第三个多。若一次把三个句子放在同一个批次中训练，然后只在最后统一调整一次权重，似乎就能更平等地考虑它们。 It was good to read some confirmation of this underlying process (though I'm sure my analogy is absurdly simplified). 读到一些对这一底层过程的确认很不错（当然，我的类比肯定极度简化了）。 The other thing that I found interesting was a mention that we would normally try to avoid overlap between batches to avoid overfitting. That sounds to me (and perhaps I'm misunderstanding) like in practice the `max_length` and the `stride` would be set to the same number. 另一个让我感兴趣的点是，书中提到我们通常会尽量避免批次之间重叠，以防止过拟合。在我看来（也许我理解错了），这意味着实践中会把 `max_length` 和 `stride` 设为相同的数字。 Anyway, that ended the section on setting up the dataset for training. Now it was on to the section on token embeddings. 无论如何，数据集设置部分到此结束。接下来是词元嵌入。 ### Token embeddings 词元嵌入 This one I was expecting to be really tricky -- how do you work out embeddings for each of the tokens in your vocabulary, or at least, how do you put things in place so that you can train them? But I was forgetting that because the embeddings are trained as part of the general LLM training, all we really needed to put in place was the infrastructure for that. 我原以为这一节会非常棘手——如何为词汇表中的每个词元计算嵌入，或者至少如何搭好可以训练它们的框架？但我忘了，嵌入会作为 LLM 总体训练的一部分被训练，所以我们真正需要准备的只是基础设施。 One interesting thing that came out of this and the various notes was why we use embeddings at all. It's relatively easy to see why you can't just feed in token IDs directly -- they're discrete numbers that don't really mean anything in and of themselves. Neural nets work best when they're dealing with some kind of continuous data, where (say) 1.5 really does mean something halfway between 1 and 2. But if "once" is token 123, and "more" is token 124, what does 123.5 mean? Nothing meaningful. 这一节和相关笔记让我明白了为什么要使用嵌入。很容易看出，不能直接把词元 ID 输入网络——它们是离散数字，本身没有真正的含义。神经网络处理某种连续数据时效果最好，比如 1.5 确实表示介于 1 和 2 之间的某个值。但如果“once”是词元 123，“more”是词元 124，那么 123.5 表示什么？没有任何有意义的东西。 I'd read in the past about "one-hot" encodings to work around issues like this, where you have discrete inputs. That's where you have a vector of length *n*, where *n* is the number of options for a choice -- you fill it with zeros, apart from one specific element that is 1, representing the particular choice in this case. It crops up in Jeremy Howard's Fast.AI course, for example -- IIRC it's specifically the case where he's working through building a system to predict who survived the Titanic, and one of the features he's looking at is the class of the passenger: first, second or third. He explains that this is a bad feature, because there's no (for example) 2.5th class, so he creates new `is_first_class`, `is_second_class`, and `is_third_class` synthetic features. You can think of that as being adding on a new feature `class` which is a vector with three elements, which is set to `[1, 0, 0]` for first class, `[0, 1, 0]` for second, and `[0, 0, 1]` for third. That is more meaningful because fractions start meaning something. Let's say that your model wanted to express "second class passengers were more likely to survive, then first, then third", it could multiply the passenger's one-hot encoded `class` vector by `[0.3, 0.5, 0.1]`. 我以前读过用“独热”（one-hot）编码来处理这类离散输入。做法是创建一个长度为 *n* 的向量，*n* 是选项数量；除了代表当前选项的某一个元素设为 1 外，其余全部设为 0。例如 Jeremy Howard 的 Fast.AI 课程就用过这种方法——如果我没记错，他是在构建预测泰坦尼克号乘客生还情况的系统时讲到的，其中一个特征是乘客舱位：一等、二等或三等。他解释说这是个糟糕的特征，因为不存在（比如）2.5 等舱，所以创建了 `is_first_class`、`is_second_class` 和 `is_third_class` 这几个合成特征。你可以把它理解为增加一个名为 `class` 的新特征，它是一个三元素向量：一等舱为 `[1, 0, 0]`，二等舱为 `[0, 1, 0]`，三等舱为 `[0, 0, 1]`。这样更有意义，因为分数开始代表某种含义。假设模型想表达“二等舱乘客的生还率更高，其次是一等舱，再次是三等舱”，它可以将乘客独热编码后的 `class` 向量乘以 `[0.3, 0.5, 0.1]`。 So, I'd had a vague thought in the past that perhaps LLMs received each token as a one-hot vector -- that is, each token was a vector as long as the vocab size, with a single `1` in the position related to its token ID, and `0`s everywhere else. This would then be fed into the LLM, which could make better sense of them. Let's say that token 1001 was "also" and 3109 was "additionally" -- they have very similar meanings, and some part of the network that was trying to deal with that kind of concept could have weights that were high for the 1001st and 3109th positions in these one-hot vectors and low everywhere else. 我过去曾模糊地想过，也许 LLM 接收到的每个词元都是独热向量——向量长度等于词汇表大小，和词元 ID 对应的位置为 1，其他位置全为 0。然后把它输入 LLM，网络就能更好地理解。比如词元 1001 是“also”，3109 是“additionally”；它们含义非常相近，网络中负责处理这类概念的某些部分，可能会在独热向量的第 1001 和 3109 个位置设置较高权重，其他位置设置较低权重。 However, in a side note, Raschka points out that this is essentially the same as the embedding system. If you take those one-hot vectors and pass them through a single fully-connected layer of neurons, you are performing the same calculations as you would to generate the embeddings. So -- embeddings here are just a neat way of creating an easily-trainable input layer. This makes a lot of intuitive sense to me, but I need to think it through to make sure I really do understand it -- something about it feels like there's an extra order involved -- order in the sense that vectors are order 1, matrices order 2, and so on -- that doesn't exactly match my mental model of how data flows through a neural network. But still, an intuitive "OK, that sort of kind of makes sense" is what I need right now. 不过，Raschka 在旁注中指出，这本质上和嵌入系统相同。如果把这些独热向量通过一个全连接神经元层，就执行了与生成嵌入相同的计算。因此，这里的嵌入只是创建易于训练的输入层的一种巧妙方式。这对我来说直觉上很合理，但还需要想一想以确保真正理解——某些地方感觉多了一层“阶数”，这里的阶数是指向量为一阶、矩阵为二阶，依此类推；这和我心中数据流过神经网络的模型不完全一致。不过，目前一个直觉上的“好吧，大概有点道理”就够了。 All that aside: the goal with embeddings was to have a set of vectors of some particular dimensionality (you might remember from the [last post](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2) that the 124M parameter GPT-2's had 768 dimensions and GPT-3 had 12,288). Each token would have one specific vector associated with it, so the process for getting the text into the LLM would look something like this pseudocode: 撇开这些不谈：嵌入的目标是得到一组具有特定维度的向量（你可能还记得[上一篇文章](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-2)提到，拥有 1.24 亿参数的 GPT-2 有 768 维，而 GPT-3 有 12,288 维）。每个词元都有一个对应的特定向量，因此把文本送入 LLM 的过程大致可以写成下面的伪代码： `tokens = tokenizer.encode(input_text) embeddings = [embeddings_dict[token] for token in tokens] result = do_LLM(embeddings)` ...where `embeddings_dict` would just have a map from each token ID to its associated embedding vector. Indeed, when I started reading the explanatory text I was expecting to see exactly that code -- a bunch of PyTorch vectors, each with the `requires_grad` property set to make them trainable. 其中 `embeddings_dict` 只是把每个词元 ID 映射到对应嵌入向量的字典。事实上，开始读解释文字时，我以为会看到的正是这段代码——一堆 PyTorch 向量，每个向量都设置 `requires_grad` 属性以便训练。 As it turns out, though, PyTorch has a `torch.nn.Embedding` class that handles that for you. From [the docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Embedding.html) it looks like it's not much more than a wrapper around the kind of dictionary I was thinking about -- though I can easily imagine that having it exist as a more abstract entity allows optimisations that make it faster than a lower-level implementation would. 但事实证明，PyTorch 有一个 `torch.nn.Embedding` 类替你处理这些工作。从[文档](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Embedding.html)来看，它似乎不比我想象的那种字典复杂多少——不过我很容易想象，作为更抽象的实体存在，可以进行优化，使其比低层实现更快。 So, the code that Rashka goes through gives a few simple examples with low numbers of dimensions just to make the concepts clear. Raschka 讲解的代码用低维度给出了几个简单示例，以便把概念讲清楚。 And next, it was on to encoding token positions. 接下来就是对词元位置进行编码。 ### Encoding word positions 编码词语位置 The core here is that the self-attention mechanism (that magical thing I'm so looking forward to learning about!) does not apparently "understand" the concept of ordering -- if it gets the same token twice in a stream it will treat it the same way each time. So in: 核心在于，自注意力机制（那个我非常期待学习的神奇机制！）似乎并不“理解”顺序概念——如果输入流中同一个词元出现两次，它每次都会以相同方式处理。因此在： ``` The cat ate the Christmas turkey ``` ...the two "the"s would be treated the same, which is obviously not what we want, as they relate to "cat" and "Christmas turkey" respectively. ……两个“the”会被当成相同的词元，这显然不是我们想要的，因为它们分别对应“cat”和“Christmas turkey”。 So once we've worked out encodings for each token, we also need to add on information about where they are in the input. These are called position embeddings, there are two flavours -- relative and absolute -- and we simply add them element-wise to the token embeddings. It's not explained how relative position embeddings work in practice (another interesting side quest I'm very carefully avoiding), but for absolute ones, we just need another dict (or it might as well be a list) mapping from the index of a token in the input stream to a vector -- that is, position 1 in the input will always have the same position embedding, position 2 its own different one, and so on. This, of course, gives us a hard cap on the number of tokens we can accept (one of the reasons LLMs tend to have a fixed context window, I imagine). But it's simple, and apparently OpenAI's GPT models use it, so it's presumably a good way to do things :-) 所以，算出每个词元的编码后，还需要加入它们在输入中的位置信息。这些叫作位置嵌入，有相对位置和绝对位置两种，我们只需把它们按元素加到词元嵌入上。书中没有解释相对位置嵌入在实践中如何工作（又一个我正小心回避的有趣支线），但绝对位置只需要另一个字典（也可以直接用列表），把输入流中的词元索引映射到一个向量——也就是说，输入中的位置 1 始终使用同一个位置嵌入，位置 2 使用另一个固定向量，依此类推。当然，这给我们能接受的词元数量设定了硬上限（我猜这也是 LLM 往往有固定上下文窗口的原因之一）。但它很简单，而且 OpenAI 的 GPT 模型显然使用了它，所以大概是个不错的方案 :-)。 Here's some sample pseudocode: 下面是一些伪代码： `tokens = tokenizer.encode(input_text) token_embeddings = [token_embeddings_dict[token] for token in tokens] position_embeddings = [position_embeddings_list[ii] for ii in range(len(tokens))] input_embeddings = [(te + pe) for (te, pe) in zip(token_embeddings, position_embeddings)] result = do_LLM(input_embeddings)` That means that the position embeddings need to be the same dimensionality as the token embeddings, of course (because otherwise we can't do the element-wise additions in the calculations of `input_embeddings`). 这意味着位置嵌入必须与词元嵌入具有相同的维度，当然如此（否则在计算 `input_embeddings` 时无法进行按元素相加）。 But again, these are things that are trained as part of the LLM training, so we just start off with arbitrary numbers in the embedding vectors for each position -- ~say all-ones for the one for position 1, all 2s for position 2, and so on~ \[NOTE: they really are arbitrary, of the same scale as the token embeddings -- see comments below for why my original example was confusing\]. Training will adjust them appropriately. 不过同样，这些参数会作为 LLM 训练的一部分被训练，所以我们只需先给每个位置的嵌入向量填入任意数字——~比如位置 1 的向量全为 1，位置 2 的全为 2，依此类推~ [注意：它们确实是任意的，但尺度应与词元嵌入相同——请参阅下方评论，了解原例子为何会造成困惑]。训练会适当地调整它们。 ### Summary 总结 Apart from my ongoing confusion about the targets in our dataset being lists with the next token to predict at the end rather than just the next token, I think that was all pretty clear to me, and hopefully my notes are reasonably clear too :-) 除了我一直困惑为什么数据集中的目标是一个列表，末尾才放要预测的下一个词元，而不是只放下一个词元之外，我觉得一切都很清楚，也希望这些笔记足够明白 :-)。 I'm fighting hard to resist the temptation to read up on that, anyway, as I've given myself strict "no side quests" instructions for this run through the book. If I still don't understand it at the end, then I'll definitely be reading up on it. 我正在努力抵制现在就查资料的诱惑，因为这次读书我给自己定下了严格的“不搞支线任务”规则。如果读完后仍然不理解，我一定会去研究。 Next time around, it's chapter 3 -- attention mechanisms. Definitely looking forward to that one! 下一次是第 3 章——注意力机制。我绝对期待这一章！ [Here's a link to the next post in this series](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-4). [这是本系列下一篇文章的链接](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2024/12/llm-from-scratch-4)。 * * * 1. The good news is that this does indeed become clear later. The bad news is that it doesn't become clear until [part 15](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/05/llm-from-scratch-15-from-context-vectors-to-logits). [↩](#fnref-1) 好消息是，后文确实会解释清楚。坏消息是，要到[第 15 部分](https://www.gilesthomas.com/2025/05/llm-from-scratch-15-from-context-vectors-to-logits)才会讲清楚。 [↩](#fnref-1)
titleZh: 从零开始编写大型语言模型，第 3 部分
summaryZh: 整理数据，使其能够由 LLM 处理，并介绍词元嵌入和位置嵌入。
